questions.title: Hardening etcd and the API Server Before a Cluster Goes to Production
questions.prompt: A security review flags that your production cluster's Secrets are 'stored in plaintext in etcd.' You push back that they're base64-encoded, not plaintext. Explain precisely why that pushback is actually wrong, what the real fix is, and what else around etcd and the API server's request pipeline you'd insist on hardening before signing off on this cluster going to production.
questions.code:
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
  - resources: ["secrets"]
    providers:
      - aescbc:
          keys:
            - name: key1
              secret: <base64-encoded-32-byte-key>
      - identity: {}

# wired in via:
# --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/enc.yaml
# --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC

# etcd hardening (control-plane network only, mutual TLS):
# ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save backup.db \
#   --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
#   --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
#   --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
#   --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key
questions.modelAnswer: The pushback is wrong because base64 is an encoding, not a cipher — it's trivially reversible by anyone, with no key required, so anyone with raw access to the etcd data directory or a snapshot of it can read every Secret in the cluster in plain text just by decoding it. The actual fix is an EncryptionConfiguration resource that tells the API server to encrypt specific resource types, Secrets included, before writing them to etcd, wired in with --encryption-provider-config on the API server. That only protects resources written going forward, though — existing Secrets need a one-time rewrite, such as reading and replacing every Secret across all namespaces, to actually get re-saved through the new encryption provider. Beyond that single fix, I'd insist on hardening the full request pipeline and etcd's exposure before sign-off. Every request to the API server passes through authentication (certs, tokens, or OIDC), then authorization — RBAC plus the Node authorizer, with --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC as the standard ordering since authorizers are checked in sequence — and then an admission control chain including NamespaceLifecycle, LimitRanger, ServiceAccount, PodSecurity, NodeRestriction, and ResourceQuota, each catching something authorization alone wouldn't. For etcd specifically, its client port 2379 and peer port 2380 should be firewalled to control-plane nodes only, with mutual TLS on both client and peer traffic. And critically, encryption at rest has to be in place before any snapshot is taken for backup, because an unencrypted etcd snapshot is exactly as readable as the live store — backing it up doesn't add protection the live database didn't already lack.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd correct the pushback directly: base64 isn't encryption, it's just a reversible text encoding with no key involved, so if anyone gets hold of the raw etcd data directory, or even just a snapshot of it, they can decode every Secret in the cluster without needing to break anything. That's the actual vulnerability the reviewer is pointing at, even if they didn't name the mechanism precisely. The real fix is EncryptionConfiguration plus --encryption-provider-config on the API server, and I'd flag immediately that this only covers Secrets written after it's turned on — anything already in etcd needs a one-time rewrite to actually get re-encrypted. But I wouldn't stop there before signing off. I'd want to see the full request pipeline locked down — authentication, then RBAC plus the Node authorizer in the right order, then the admission chain doing its job, NodeRestriction specifically so a compromised node can't relabel itself into a more privileged pool. And I'd want etcd itself firewalled off entirely — only the API server should ever reach ports 2379 and 2380, and that traffic needs to be mutual TLS, not just TLS one direction. The thing I'd push hardest on is sequencing: encryption at rest has to be live before anyone takes a backup snapshot, because an unencrypted snapshot is just as exposed as the live database — backing it up too early doesn't protect anything.
commonMistakes: Accepts base64 encoding as a form of encryption, missing that it requires no key and is trivially reversible
Enables EncryptionConfiguration going forward but forgets existing Secrets need a one-time rewrite
Secures RBAC but ignores the admission control chain and Node authorizer as separate protections
Leaves etcd's client/peer ports reachable beyond the control-plane network
Takes an etcd snapshot backup before encryption at rest is actually in place, leaving the backup just as exposed

Describes the EncryptionConfiguration/--encryption-provider-config fix and its forward-only scope
Explains the authn -> authz (Node,RBAC) -> admission control request pipeline correctly
Lists concrete etcd network/access hardening (port restriction to control-plane, mutual TLS)
Explains why encryption at rest must precede snapshotting, not follow it

questions.title: GitOps Repo Structure and a Guarded Prod Sync Policy
questions.prompt: A platform team runs one GitOps config repo with Kustomize base+overlays for dev/staging/prod. Dev and staging auto-sync, and so did prod — a bad PR merged into the prod overlay path and ArgoCD applied it automatically outside business hours, causing an outage. As the architect fixing this: write the ArgoCD Application manifests for dev and prod so dev/staging keep fast automated convergence, while prod requires an explicit human sync action but still surfaces drift the instant it exists (not just after someone remembers to check). Then explain the extra gate you'd add at the Git layer itself.
questions.code:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: payments-api-dev
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/acme/gitops-config.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: apps/payments-api/overlays/dev
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: payments-dev
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true
---
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: payments-api-prod
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/acme/gitops-config.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: apps/payments-api/overlays/prod
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: payments-prod
  syncPolicy:
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true
  # No automated block: ArgoCD still computes Sync status on its normal
  # reconciliation loop and will show OutOfSync immediately, but will
  # never auto-apply. A human must run `argocd app sync payments-api-prod`.
questions.example:
# .github/CODEOWNERS
# A second human gate BEFORE a merge can even reach the prod overlay path
apps/payments-api/overlays/prod/ @platform-leads @sre-oncall
questions.modelAnswer: The incident happened because the prod Application had `syncPolicy.automated` enabled, so the moment the bad PR merged into the path ArgoCD watches, it was synced and applied with no gate. The fix isn't to stop ArgoCD from tracking prod at all — it's to split sync detection from sync application. Each environment gets its own Application pointing at its own Kustomize overlay path and destination namespace. Dev and staging keep `automated: { prune: true, selfHeal: true }` because fast, unattended convergence is exactly what you want there — a bad dev deploy costs nothing. Prod's Application omits the `automated` block entirely. ArgoCD's reconciliation loop still runs on its default interval and still computes Sync status by diffing live state against Git, so the moment someone merges to the prod overlay, the Application flips to `OutOfSync` and is visible on the dashboard — nothing about removing `automated` disables detection, only auto-apply. Someone then has to explicitly run `argocd app sync payments-api-prod` or click Sync in the UI, which is the deliberate human gate the incident was missing. I'd pair that with a CODEOWNERS rule on the prod overlay path so a merge to it itself requires a second reviewer before it even reaches 'OutOfSync' status, adding a gate before the gate. `prune` matters less for prod day-to-day, but I'd still require an explicit flag on manual syncs that intend to delete resources, so a stale manifest removal doesn't surprise anyone either.
questions.professionalAnswer: Honestly, the root cause here is that someone treated 'automated sync' as the default for every environment without thinking about what each one is actually for. I'd walk the team through it this way: dev and staging exist so that merging to main converges fast and nobody waits around — keep selfHeal and prune on there, that's the whole value of GitOps. Prod is different, and the mistake was giving it the same policy. So I split it into its own Application with no automated block at all. What a lot of people don't realize is that doesn't turn off drift detection — ArgoCD keeps diffing prod against Git on its normal loop and will still flag OutOfSync the instant something changes, you just don't get an automatic apply. A human still has to run the sync. I'd also push back on relying on that alone, though — I'd add a CODEOWNERS entry on the prod overlay directory so the PR itself needs a second approver before it can even land, which means there are now two separate humans involved before prod actually moves: one approving the merge, one approving the sync. That's the layered gate the postmortem is going to ask for, and it costs nothing in velocity for dev and staging.
commonMistakes: Thinks removing syncPolicy.automated also stops ArgoCD from detecting drift — it only stops auto-apply, not diff computation
Conflates Sync status with Health status, assuming manual sync alone prevents a bad deploy if the app is unhealthy
Forgets prune/selfHeal still needed on dev/staging or drift accumulates there too
Puts an approval gate only in the CI pipeline instead of also protecting the config repo path, leaving a direct git push to the prod overlay un-reviewed
Assumes one Application resource can describe all three environments instead of one per environment/overlay

Sync status vs Health status are independent axes
automated block fields: prune, selfHeal
Manual sync requires explicit argocd app sync / UI action, but drift detection still runs
CODEOWNERS/branch protection on the prod overlay path as the human gate

Produces valid Application manifests per environment with correct destinations
Explains that drift detection/Sync status still functions without automated apply
Adds a real reviewer gate (CODEOWNERS/branch protection) for the prod path

questions.title: Wiring Automated Rollback into an Argo Rollouts Canary
questions.prompt: The checkout-service canary rollout pauses at fixed timers (10%, 25%, 50%, 100%) with no metric check behind the pauses. A bad deploy spiked 5xx errors overnight and sailed through every pause because no one was watching a dashboard. As the architect, rewrite the Rollout and its AnalysisTemplate(s) so error rate AND latency are checked automatically at each step, with automatic abort and traffic rollback on a bad signal — no human required.
questions.code:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: error-rate-check
spec:
  metrics:
    - name: error-rate
      interval: 1m
      successCondition: result[0] <= 0.01
      failureLimit: 2
      provider:
        prometheus:
          address: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
          query: |
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
            /
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout"}[5m]))
---
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: p95-latency-check
spec:
  metrics:
    - name: p95-latency
      interval: 1m
      successCondition: result[0] <= 0.3
      failureLimit: 2
      provider:
        prometheus:
          address: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
          query: |
            histogram_quantile(0.95,
              sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="checkout"}[5m])) by (le)
            )
---
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: checkout-service
spec:
  replicas: 10
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
        - setWeight: 10
        - analysis:
            templates:
              - templateName: error-rate-check
              - templateName: p95-latency-check
        - pause: { duration: 5m }
        - setWeight: 50
        - analysis:
            templates:
              - templateName: error-rate-check
              - templateName: p95-latency-check
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        - setWeight: 100
questions.example:
# On a breach, Argo Rollouts aborts automatically:
kubectl argo rollouts get rollout checkout-service
# STATUS: Degraded  (AnalysisRun 'error-rate-check' failed, traffic reverted to stable ReplicaSet)
questions.modelAnswer: The gap is that the original Rollout only had `pause` steps — a fixed duration with nobody and nothing actually checking the metrics behind it, so a bad deploy just waits out the timer and advances anyway. I'd replace that with Argo Rollouts' `AnalysisTemplate` mechanism, which runs a real Prometheus query on an interval and compares it against a threshold automatically. I'd define two templates: one computing the 5xx-to-total request ratio over a 5-minute window with `successCondition: result[0] <= 0.01`, and a second computing p95 latency via `histogram_quantile(0.95, ...)` with its own threshold, because error rate alone misses a technically-successful-but-much-slower regression. Both get referenced in an `analysis.templates` list at each `setWeight` step in the Rollout — at 10% and at 50%, before advancing further. `interval: 1m` means the query reruns every minute, and `failureLimit: 2` means it takes two consecutive breaches, not one noisy data point, to call it a failure — that guards against a single network blip triggering a rollback. If either template's successCondition fails enough times, Argo Rollouts aborts automatically and shifts all traffic back to the last stable ReplicaSet without anyone paging on-call first. I'd still keep a short `pause` alongside the analysis at each step, since the query needs real traffic flowing at that weight to produce a meaningful sample before the threshold check means anything.
questions.professionalAnswer: What actually failed here isn't the canary strategy, it's that 'pause for five minutes' was doing the job of a human who was supposed to be watching and nobody was, especially overnight. I'd tell the team: stop treating the pause as the safety mechanism, because a timer doesn't know what the dashboards look like. I'd add an AnalysisTemplate for error rate using the same PromQL pattern from Prometheus — 5xx over total, five-minute window, must stay under 1%. But I wouldn't stop there, because in my experience a deploy that's technically correct but twice as slow is just as real a regression, so I'd add a second template watching p95 latency with its own threshold. Both get attached to the rollout's canary steps right after each setWeight, so instead of just pausing blindly, the rollout is actually asking a question at 10% and again at 50%: is this safe to keep going? If the answer's no — two consecutive failed checks, not one flaky sample — Argo Rollouts aborts on its own and flips traffic back to stable immediately. That's the whole point: it catches the bad deploy in minutes at 2am instead of someone noticing it in the morning stand-up after it already hit 100% of traffic.
commonMistakes: Only wires in error rate and ignores latency, missing 'technically correct but slower' regressions
Sets successCondition thresholds so loose nothing ever fails, or so strict normal variance triggers constant rollbacks
Replaces the pause entirely instead of keeping a short pause alongside analysis so the metric window has time to accumulate real samples
Doesn't realize analysis queries run on an interval requiring failureLimit consecutive breaches, not a single blip
Assumes automated rollback replaces chaos/game-day testing instead of complementing it
keyPoints: AnalysisTemplate structure: metric, interval, successCondition, failureLimit, Prometheus provider/query
Wiring analysis steps into canary steps alongside setWeight/pause
Multiple signals (error rate + latency) checked per step
Automatic abort shifts traffic back to the stable ReplicaSet without human action
Thresholds must be tuned to avoid both false positives and false negatives

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a correct AnalysisTemplate with a real PromQL query and threshold
Adds a second signal (latency) beyond error rate
Correctly wires analysis into canary steps at the right points
Explains failureLimit/interval semantics and automatic rollback behavior

questions.title: Enforcing a Non-Optional Security Scan Across 300 Repos
questions.prompt: A 300-repo org shares a pipeline template, but a team quietly deleted the shared security-scan step-template reference from their own azure-pipelines.yml, and it went unnoticed for months because the pipeline still ran 'successfully.' As the architect, rewrite the consuming pipeline so the scan step can no longer be silently dropped, explain the structural reason the old approach allowed it, and add the one control that makes removal actually impossible, not just discouraged.
questions.code:
# BEFORE (vulnerable): a step-level template include inside a steps: list
# steps:
#   - template: templates/build-test-scan.yml@templates
#     parameters:
#       nodeVersion: "20.x"
#   # ^ anyone can delete this one block, or add steps before/after it that
#   #   never call it, and the pipeline still runs and reports success.

# AFTER (fixed): the consuming pipeline no longer owns its own structure
resources:
  repositories:
    - repository: templates
      type: git
      name: PlatformEngineering/pipeline-templates
      ref: refs/tags/v1

extends:
  template: templates/build-test-scan.yml@templates
  parameters:
    nodeVersion: "20.x"

---
# templates repo: templates/build-test-scan.yml (unchanged, owns the required scan)
parameters:
  - name: nodeVersion
    type: string
    default: "20.x"

steps:
  - task: NodeTool@0
    inputs:
      versionSpec: ${{ parameters.nodeVersion }}
  - script: npm ci
  - script: npm test
  - script: npm audit --audit-level=high
    displayName: "Required security scan"
questions.example:
# Equivalent GitHub Actions version for repos hosted there, version-pinned not @main
jobs:
  run-shared-pipeline:
    uses: my-org/pipeline-templates/.github/workflows/build-test-scan.yml@v1
    with:
      node-version: "20"
    secrets:
      NPM_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.NPM_TOKEN }}
questions.modelAnswer: The actual vulnerability wasn't the shared template itself — it's that the consuming repo's azure-pipelines.yml included it as a `steps`-level template reference inside a `steps:` list. That form is composable, which is exactly its weakness here: anyone editing the file can delete that one block, or add steps before and after it, and the pipeline still runs and reports success with no scan ever executed, because nothing about a step-level include stops the surrounding file from rearranging itself. The fix is to switch the consuming pipeline from a steps-level include to `extends:` at the top of the file, referencing the templates repo through `resources.repositories` pinned to `ref: refs/tags/v1`. `extends` changes the ownership model: the consuming pipeline is no longer free to define its own step list around the template's steps — the template's structure is what runs, full stop. A team can still pass in the `nodeVersion` parameter the template exposes, but it can't quietly drop the `npm audit` step, because that step isn't theirs to remove. I'd pair this with a required branch-protection status check naming the scan job specifically, so even if someone hand-edits the YAML to stop calling the template at all, the PR can't merge without that check passing. Pinning to a tag rather than the templates repo's default branch also matters — it keeps every consumer's build reproducible and immune to an unreviewed change landing on main.
questions.professionalAnswer: When I dug into this, the tell is always the same: the pipeline 'worked', it just quietly stopped doing one of the things it was supposed to do, and nobody got an error because nothing was technically broken. That's what a steps-level template include lets happen — it's just another block in a list, and lists are easy to edit around. So the fix I'd push for isn't a patch to that one repo, it's changing the pattern: move to `extends` instead of a step-level template. The difference in practice is that with `extends`, the consuming pipeline stops owning its own shape — it inherits the template's steps as a whole, parameters and all, and can't selectively drop the scan step the way it could when the template was just one item in its own steps list. I'd also pin the template reference to a tag, not the template repo's main branch, so nobody upstream can change behavior under me without me choosing to bump the version. And honestly, I wouldn't trust the YAML alone to hold — I'd add a required status check on that scan job in branch protection, because the real lesson from this incident is that 'the pipeline file says it runs' and 'it's actually enforced' turned out to be two different things.
commonMistakes: Uses a step/job-level template: include instead of extends:, leaving the consuming file free to add steps around it or drop it entirely
Pins the templates repo reference to a branch instead of a tag, so a change to the template silently alters every consumer's build without a version bump
Believes fixing the YAML alone is sufficient and skips adding a branch-protection required status check
Keeps special-case conditionals inside the shared template for individual teams instead of exposing them as named parameters
Assumes GitHub reusable workflows and Azure DevOps extends provide an identical guarantee, missing that extends is the stronger structural control
keyPoints: step/job template: vs extends: — the structural difference in what a consumer can override
extends means the consumer cannot skip or reorder the template's defined steps
Version pinning (ref: refs/tags/v1, @v1) vs tracking a moving default branch
GitHub Actions reusable workflow (workflow_call) is the equivalent write-once-call-everywhere mechanism
A required status check on the real template job is what makes silent removal actually impossible

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Diagnoses that a step-level template inclusion is what let the scan be silently removed
Correctly rewrites the pipeline to use extends with a version-pinned template reference
Explains the structural guarantee extends provides over a steps/jobs template
Adds a real additional control (branch protection / required check) rather than relying on YAML alone

questions.title: A Terraform Module That Provisions a Network on Either Cloud
questions.prompt: A landing-zone team wants one reusable Terraform module for the network layer that a workload team can call with cloud = "azure" or cloud = "aws" and get a consistent network_id output either way, without maintaining two separate modules. Write the module (variables, both resource branches, unified output) and a root-module call. Then a second workload needs a critical config replicated to BOTH clouds simultaneously, not a choice — show why you can't just set cloud = "both" inside the same module, and what structurally different pattern that actually requires.
questions.modelAnswer: This needs two genuinely different Terraform patterns, and conflating them is the mistake to avoid. For 'pick one cloud per deployment,' I'd write a module that declares both resource blocks — `azurerm_virtual_network` and `aws_vpc` — and uses `count = var.cloud == "azure" ? 1 : 0` (and the inverse for AWS) so exactly one branch actually provisions anything; Terraform creates zero instances of the other branch and they don't exist in state. Both branches feed a single `output "network_id"` block that returns the right resource's id regardless of which branch ran, so the calling code never needs its own cloud-aware branching; the module already normalized that away. I'd nest this inside a dedicated child module and thread `var.cloud` down from the root exactly once rather than repeating the ternary everywhere. For the second requirement — replicating a config to both clouds on every apply, not choosing one — that's not a `count` problem at all, because you genuinely want both resources created every time, with no conditional. That calls for provider aliasing: declare a second provider instance, e.g. `provider "aws" { alias = "secondary" }`, and reference it explicitly per resource with `provider = aws.secondary`. You can't set `cloud = "both"` inside the count-per-cloud module and expect it to work, because `count` is fundamentally an either/or mechanism; dual-provisioning needs two resources living in the same state with no branching logic involved at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by pointing out these are actually two different problems wearing the same 'multi-cloud Terraform' label. The first one — give me a network on whichever cloud I pick — I'd solve with a module that has both an `azurerm_virtual_network` block and an `aws_vpc` block sitting right next to each other, each gated by `count` keyed off a `cloud` variable, so only one of them ever actually creates anything on a given apply. The trick that makes it actually reusable is giving both branches the same output name, so whoever calls the module just reads `network_id` and doesn't care which cloud produced it — that's the real portability win, not the module itself. I'd wrap that in a child module and pass `cloud` down from the root once, instead of letting `var.cloud == "azure" ? ... : ...` spread through every resource. Now, if someone comes to me asking for `cloud = "both"` because they want the config replicated everywhere, I'd stop them right there — that's not a count problem anymore, because count is inherently 'exactly one of these.' What they actually need is a second provider block with an alias, and a resource that explicitly says `provider = aws.secondary`, so both resources get created on every single apply with no conditional logic involved. Different intent, different mechanism — mixing them up is how people end up fighting Terraform instead of using it.
commonMistakes: Tries to make cloud = "both" work inside the count-per-cloud module instead of recognizing dual-provisioning needs a structurally different root-level design
Puts var.cloud == "azure" ? ... : ... ternaries inside every attribute of a shared resource block instead of using count to create zero or one of each cloud's dedicated block
Forgets to reference count-indexed resources with [0], causing a plan error when count is used
Assumes a root module's var.cloud variable automatically threads through child modules without explicitly passing it as an argument to each module block
Believes one resource type can 'become' another provider's resource type rather than understanding both must be declared and selected via count
keyPoints: count = var.cloud == "x" ? 1 : 0 pattern for conditional single-cloud provisioning
Unified output name across both branches for a portable module contract
Child module composition passing var.cloud down once
Provider aliasing (provider = aws.secondary) for genuine dual-cloud applies, a different mechanism than count branching
Why one resource type can never become another provider's resource type at apply time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct count-per-cloud module structure with both resource branches
Unified output across both branches
Correctly distinguishes provider aliasing (dual-provision) from count branching (single-choice)
Clean child-module composition passing var.cloud through

questions.title: Standing Up a Resilient Azure-to-AWS Cross-Cloud Tunnel
questions.prompt: A data-replication job between an Azure VNet and an AWS VPC runs over a single VPN tunnel configured with static routes, and it breaks every time either side's subnets change because nobody remembers to update the route tables. As the architect, rebuild the connection with dynamic routing so address-space changes propagate automatically, then explain the second, structurally different path you'd add for real resilience — and why it isn't just "add more bandwidth."
questions.code:
# Azure side: a local network gateway representing the AWS VPN endpoint
az network local-gateway create \
  --resource-group hub-rg \
  --name aws-vpc-gateway \
  --gateway-ip-address 52.14.88.201 \
  --local-address-prefixes 10.50.0.0/16

az network vpn-connection create \
  --resource-group hub-rg \
  --name azure-to-aws \
  --vnet-gateway1 azure-vpn-gw \
  --local-gateway2 aws-vpc-gateway \
  --shared-key "<pre-shared-key>" \
  --enable-bgp true

# AWS side (conceptually equivalent, run via aws cli/console):
# 1. Create a customer gateway pointing at the Azure VPN Gateway's public IP
# 2. Attach a VPN connection with BGP enabled to the VPC's virtual private gateway
# Both ends now exchange routes dynamically instead of relying on
# hand-maintained static route tables.
questions.example:
# For sustained, throughput-sensitive replication traffic, pair the VPN
# with a colocation meet-point as the primary path and the VPN as failover:
# ExpressRoute circuit + Direct Connect connection cross-connected in the
# same connectivity-provider facility, entirely off the public internet.
# If that dedicated circuit degrades, routing fails over to the VPN tunnel
# at reduced throughput instead of a hard outage.
questions.modelAnswer: The outage pattern described — the tunnel breaking every time either side's subnets change — is the signature of static routing, not a flaky tunnel. I'd rebuild the connection with BGP enabled so each gateway learns the other's address space dynamically instead of a human maintaining a route table by hand. On the Azure side: `az network local-gateway create` to represent the AWS Virtual Private Gateway's public IP and the AWS-side address prefixes, then `az network vpn-connection create --vnet-gateway1 azure-vpn-gw --local-gateway2 aws-vpc-gateway --shared-key <psk> --enable-bgp true`. On the AWS side, a matching customer gateway pointed at the Azure VPN Gateway's public IP, attached to the VPC's virtual private gateway through a VPN connection with BGP enabled as well. Once both ends run BGP, a subnet added on either side propagates automatically — no more manual route edits, no more outages tied to someone forgetting to update a static route. For resilience beyond that single tunnel, I wouldn't just add a second VPN tunnel and call it done — I'd evaluate a colocation meet-point: an ExpressRoute circuit and a Direct Connect connection cross-connected in the same facility, off the public internet, for the sustained replication traffic. The VPN tunnel then becomes the failover path if that dedicated circuit degrades, routing fails over to it at reduced throughput instead of a hard outage. That's resilience through two structurally different paths, not just two copies of the same one.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd flag is that this isn't really a 'the VPN is unreliable' problem, it's a 'nobody turned on BGP' problem — static routes between two clouds are basically guaranteed to drift the moment either side's network changes, because a human has to remember to go update them. So step one is rebuilding the tunnel with BGP on both ends: the local network gateway on Azure representing AWS's endpoint, the customer gateway on AWS representing Azure's, and `--enable-bgp true` on the connection itself, so route exchange happens automatically from then on. That alone fixes the outage pattern they described. But I wouldn't stop there for something a replication job actually depends on — one tunnel is still one path. I'd look at whether the traffic volume justifies a colocation meet-point, a private cross-connect between an ExpressRoute circuit and a Direct Connect connection, which is the right call for sustained, throughput-sensitive traffic like ongoing replication. And I'd keep the VPN tunnel around, not retire it, specifically as the failover path if that dedicated circuit has a problem — so you get graceful degradation instead of an outage. That's a deliberate two-path design, not just throwing more bandwidth at it.
commonMistakes: Relies on static routes instead of enabling BGP, so any address-space change requires manually re-editing routes
Assumes a single VPN tunnel is sufficient for 'resilience' without a second independent path
Treats the colocation meet-point and the VPN as mutually exclusive instead of recognizing the VPN's value as a failover path for the meet-point
Forgets each side needs a matching gateway object representing the other side's endpoint, not just a generic 'VPN resource'
Confuses 'redundancy' with 'more throughput,' missing that the goal is failover during degradation, not raw bandwidth
keyPoints: Azure VPN Gateway <-> AWS Virtual Private Gateway tunnel via local/customer gateway pairing
BGP over the tunnel enables dynamic route exchange instead of manual static routes
Colocation meet-point (ExpressRoute + Direct Connect cross-connect) for sustained high-throughput traffic, off the public internet
VPN as a failover path for a meet-point circuit — redundancy via two different mechanisms
Choosing VPN-only vs VPN+meet-point based on traffic pattern, not preference

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct az CLI for local-gateway + vpn-connection with --enable-bgp true
Explains why BGP fixes the original static-route fragility
Proposes a second independent path (meet-point) with correct rationale
Articulates resilience as failover design, not just bandwidth

questions.title: One Governance Control, Enforced the Same Way on Every Cloud
questions.prompt: The org's rule "no storage resource is ever publicly readable" exists three times — an Azure Policy definition, an AWS SCP, and an on-prem change-control checklist item. A new storage SKU shipped on one cloud and the native rule there was never updated to cover it, going unenforced for six months until an audit caught it. As the architect, write an OPA/Rego policy that blocks a non-compliant Terraform plan for BOTH azurerm_storage_account and aws_s3_bucket before it ever reaches either cloud's API, and explain what native Azure Policy/AWS Config still has to keep doing even after this policy-as-code layer exists.
questions.code:
package main

deny[msg] {
  some rc
  rc := input.resource_changes[_]
  rc.type == "azurerm_storage_account"
  rc.change.after.allow_nested_items_to_be_public == true
  msg := sprintf("Azure storage account %v allows public blob access", [rc.address])
}

deny[msg] {
  some rc
  rc := input.resource_changes[_]
  rc.type == "aws_s3_bucket"
  acl := rc.change.after.acl
  acl == "public-read"
  msg := sprintf("AWS S3 bucket %v has a public ACL (%v)", [rc.address, acl])
}

deny[msg] {
  some rc
  rc := input.resource_changes[_]
  rc.type == "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block"
  rc.change.after.block_public_acls == false
  msg := sprintf("S3 public access block %v leaves block_public_acls disabled", [rc.address])
}
questions.example:
# CI gate, run against the plan before apply:
terraform plan -out plan.tfplan
terraform show -json plan.tfplan > plan.json
conftest test -p policy/ plan.json
# A deny[] match fails the pipeline before terraform apply ever runs,
# regardless of which cloud the plan targets.
questions.modelAnswer: The actual failure mode here is structural: maintaining the same control as three independent native rule sets guarantees drift eventually, because nobody owns keeping all three in sync when something changes, and a new storage SKU is exactly the kind of change that falls through. I'd address it by writing one shared control as code instead of three native definitions, using Open Policy Agent's Rego language evaluated against the Terraform plan output (via conftest, or Sentinel if the pipeline is Terraform Cloud/Enterprise). The policy walks resource_changes in the plan JSON and denies anything that would create public storage, regardless of which cloud it targets: for azurerm_storage_account, deny if allow_nested_items_to_be_public is true; for AWS, deny both a public ACL on aws_s3_bucket and a disabled block_public_acls on the associated aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block, since either one alone can leave a bucket exposed. This runs in CI against every plan before apply, so a non-compliant change for either cloud is blocked at the same stage, written once. Crucially, I would not retire Azure Policy or AWS Config — resources created outside Terraform, through the portal, an emergency console change, or a script, never go through a plan at all, so native, always-on enforcement still has to catch those continuously after the fact. The real fix isn't picking one enforcement layer over the other; it's making sure the intent is defined once, in the policy-as-code layer, and mapped to each environment's native mechanism for everything Terraform doesn't touch.
questions.professionalAnswer: Honestly, the pattern in this story is depressingly predictable — three teams each maintaining their own copy of 'no public storage' in three different syntaxes, and the moment any one of them doesn't notice a new SKU, the rule silently has a hole in it nobody's watching for. I wouldn't try to fix that by writing a better Azure Policy definition or a better SCP — I'd write the control once, as a Rego policy, and run it against the Terraform plan before anything ever applies. Concretely: walk the plan's resource changes, and for any azurerm_storage_account or aws_s3_bucket that would end up publicly readable — including the easy-to-miss aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block override — fail the plan right there in CI. One file, one intent, enforced identically regardless of which cloud the resource is headed for. What I'd be careful to say in the review, though, is that this doesn't mean Azure Policy and AWS Config go away. They're still the only thing watching resources that never went through Terraform at all — someone clicking around in the portal, an emergency fix from the console. So I'd frame it as: policy-as-code catches it at provisioning time, native policy keeps watching everything else, and the control itself only has to be written down once instead of three times that inevitably drift apart.
commonMistakes: Writes a separate Rego policy per cloud instead of one policy expressing the shared intent evaluated against whichever resource type appears in the plan
Thinks the OPA/Sentinel layer replaces Azure Policy and AWS Config entirely instead of understanding it only catches provisioning done through Terraform
Checks only the obvious acl attribute on S3 and misses aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block, which can override a seemingly-safe bucket
Hardcodes the check against today's known attributes without anticipating a new SKU/attribute shipping later — the exact failure mode in the scenario
Gates terraform apply after the fact instead of gating the plan in CI, catching drift after it happens instead of preventing it
keyPoints: One control catalog entry, one shared policy-as-code evaluation, vs maintaining three native rule sets that drift apart
OPA/Rego (or Sentinel) evaluating a Terraform plan before apply
Policy-as-code is a layer above native enforcement, not a replacement for it
Native Azure Policy / AWS Config still has to cover resources created outside Terraform
Why triplicated native rules silently drift when a new resource type/SKU ships

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Writes a working Rego policy covering both azurerm_storage_account and aws_s3_bucket
Correctly wires it to gate terraform plan in CI before apply
Explains why this doesn't retire native Azure Policy/AWS Config
Identifies the real drift mechanism (new SKU/attribute untracked in one native rule set)

questions.title: Provisioning a Spot-Capable GPU Training VM Across Two Clouds
questions.prompt: An ML platform team wants Terraform to provision an A100 training VM on whichever cloud has capacity, defaulting to spot/low-priority pricing to control cost. Write the Terraform (Azure NC-series and AWS P-series) including the spot configuration on each, and the pre-flight quota checks you'd run before ever attempting the apply. Then explain why GPU spot eviction is a materially different risk than general-purpose spot for a training workload specifically.
questions.example:
# Spot GPU is only usable for training paired with checkpointing + an
# orchestrator that reacts to the eviction notice:
# ~2-minute reclaim window -> checkpoint on notice -> relaunch from last
# checkpoint, same instance_market_options config, new VM.
questions.modelAnswer: Before writing any HCL, I'd check GPU quota on both clouds, because this fails at apply time otherwise, after everything else is correct: `az vm list-usage --location eastus -o table` looking for the `NCADSA100v4 Family vCPUs` line, and on AWS checking the Service Quotas console (or `aws service-quotas get-service-quota`) for the P-series on-demand vCPU limit in the target region — quota is regional, so an approval in one region doesn't help a config targeting another. For the Terraform itself, the resource types don't change from the non-GPU course — `azurerm_linux_virtual_machine` sized `Standard_NC24ads_A100_v4`, and `aws_instance` as `p4d.24xlarge` using the Deep Learning AMI lookup — only the spot configuration is new. On Azure, that means `priority = "Spot"`, an `eviction_policy` of `Delete`, and `max_bid_price = -1` to pay up to the on-demand price rather than capping it and risking an avoidable eviction. On AWS, `instance_market_options { market_type = "spot" spot_options { spot_instance_type = "one-time" } }`. The part I'd flag hardest to the team: GPU spot capacity is reclaimed far more aggressively than general-purpose spot, because GPU capacity is scarcer overall, and losing a GPU spot instance mid-training loses hours of expensive sunk compute, not minutes like a CPU batch job would. Spot is only genuinely usable here if there's a checkpointing strategy — regular checkpoints plus an orchestrator that checkpoints on the eviction notice and relaunches — sitting on top of this Terraform config, not a substitute for it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd insist on before anyone writes a line of Terraform is checking quota first, because I've watched a perfectly correct GPU config fail at apply time simply because the subscription had zero quota for that VM family in that region — and quota approval doesn't travel between regions, so you have to check it where you're actually deploying. Once that's cleared, the resource blocks themselves are the same ones from the regular compute course, azurerm_linux_virtual_machine and aws_instance, just sized up — Standard_NC24ads_A100_v4 on Azure, p4d.24xlarge on AWS with the Deep Learning AMI. The spot piece is where I'd spend the real conversation. On Azure that's priority = "Spot" with an eviction policy and a bid price; on AWS it's the instance_market_options block. But I'd push back hard if the team treats this like CPU spot — GPU capacity gets reclaimed much more aggressively because it's so much scarcer, and if you're mid-training when that eviction notice lands, you can lose hours of genuinely expensive compute, not a few minutes of a batch job. So spot only makes sense here paired with real checkpointing and an orchestrator that reacts to the eviction notice and relaunches from the last checkpoint. Without that, I'd actually recommend on-demand for anything long-running, even at the higher cost.
commonMistakes: Requests GPU capacity without checking quota first, so terraform apply fails after everything else was correct
Treats GPU spot eviction risk the same as general-purpose spot, not accounting for how much more aggressively GPU capacity is reclaimed
Uses priority = "Spot" without an eviction_policy/max_bid_price strategy or without a checkpointing mechanism, losing hours of sunk training cost on eviction
Assumes any region has the GPU family available without checking (az vm list-skus), writing a config that fails at a region that doesn't carry that SKU
Forgets quota requests are scoped per region, so approval in one region doesn't help a config targeting a different one
keyPoints: GPU quota is a pre-flight check (az vm list-usage, Service Quotas), not a Terraform concern
Azure spot config: priority = "Spot", eviction_policy, max_bid_price
AWS spot config: instance_market_options.spot_options
GPU spot eviction is more aggressive than general-purpose spot; needs checkpointing + relaunch orchestration to be usable for training
Regional GPU family availability must be checked before writing the config

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct Azure spot VM Terraform fields on the right size
Correct AWS spot Terraform on the right instance type
Identifies and performs the pre-flight quota check before apply
Explains the aggressive-eviction risk and the checkpointing mitigation needed for spot training

questions.title: Choosing and Configuring GPU Sharing for a Mixed Inference Workload
questions.prompt: A cluster has 4 A100s. Three small inference services each use about 10% of a GPU's memory/compute; a fourth tenant is a sensitive multi-tenant workload that legally cannot share memory or a fault domain with anyone else. Configure GPU sharing correctly for both cases — the right mechanism for the three light services, a different mechanism for the isolated tenant — and justify which goes where.
questions.code:
# Node pool A (3 light inference services) — time-slicing
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: nvidia-device-plugin-config
  namespace: kube-system
data:
  config.yaml: |
    version: v1
    sharing:
      timeSlicing:
        resources:
          - name: nvidia.com/gpu
            replicas: 4
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: inference-service-a
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: model-server
          image: registry/inference-a:v3
          resources:
            limits:
              nvidia.com/gpu: 1
---
# Node pool B (isolated tenant) — MIG, enabled once per node:
# nvidia-smi -mig 1
# nvidia-smi mig -cgi 19,19,19 -C   (profile IDs vary; `nvidia-smi mig -lgip` lists what's available)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: isolated-tenant-inference
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: model-server
          image: registry/inference-isolated:v3
          resources:
            limits:
              nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb: 1
questions.example:
# At scale, manage MIG partitioning declaratively across a node pool
# instead of running nvidia-smi by hand on every node:
# NVIDIA GPU Operator's `mig.strategy` setting.
questions.modelAnswer: These are two different problems masquerading as one 'GPU sharing' request, and using the same mechanism for both would be wrong for the isolated tenant specifically. For the three light inference services, each using roughly 10% of an A100, time-slicing is the right fit: I'd configure the NVIDIA device plugin via a ConfigMap setting sharing.timeSlicing.resources with replicas: 4 for nvidia.com/gpu, which makes one physical GPU advertise as 4 schedulable units. Each service's Deployment then just requests nvidia.com/gpu: 1 as normal, and the GPU's hardware scheduler context-switches between them. The explicit tradeoff I'd accept here: no memory or fault isolation, so a runaway process in one of those three could, in theory, affect another's memory pool — acceptable for low-stakes, forgiving inference traffic, not acceptable for the fourth tenant. For that isolated workload, I'd use Multi-Instance GPU on a separate node instead, enabling it once at the node level with nvidia-smi -mig 1 and partitioning with nvidia-smi mig -cgi (or the NVIDIA GPU Operator's mig.strategy for declarative management across a pool), then have that tenant's Deployment request a specific partition, e.g. nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb: 1. MIG gives genuine hardware-level isolation — separate memory, cache, and compute cores — which is the only mechanism that satisfies a 'cannot share a fault domain' requirement; time-slicing structurally cannot meet that bar no matter how it's tuned.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd separate these into two buckets right away instead of looking for one sharing mechanism that covers everyone, because they actually have different requirements. The three small inference services aren't sensitive about each other — they're just underusing a whole A100 each — so time-slicing is the obvious fit: turn on the device plugin's time-slicing config with four replicas per physical GPU, and each service just asks for nvidia.com/gpu: 1 like it always has, no changes to the deployment itself. I'd be upfront that this means zero isolation between them — they all share the same memory pool — but for three low-stakes services that's a fine trade for not paying for three mostly-idle GPUs. The fourth tenant is where I'd draw a hard line: if the requirement is genuinely 'cannot share a fault domain with anyone else,' time-slicing can't satisfy that no matter how carefully you tune it, because it's software scheduling on shared memory. That one needs MIG, on hardware that supports it, partitioned once at the node level and then requested by its specific profile name, like nvidia.com/mig-1g.10gb. That's real hardware isolation, not just a scheduling fairness mechanism, and it's the only one of the two that actually answers the isolation requirement rather than just being 'good enough.'
commonMistakes: Applies time-slicing to the isolated tenant, not realizing it has zero memory/fault isolation between the replicas sharing the same physical GPU
Applies MIG everywhere by default without checking the GPU/driver actually supports it or accepting the fixed-partition-layout tradeoff
Forgets both mechanisms require node-level device plugin / GPU Operator configuration, not just a pod-level resource request
Mismatches a MIG profile too small for the isolated tenant's real workload, causing OOM inside its own dedicated slice
Thinks requesting nvidia.com/gpu: 1 after enabling time-slicing still claims a whole physical GPU rather than one of the N software replicas
keyPoints: Time-slicing: software context-switching, no memory/fault isolation, good for light/bursty inference
MIG: hardware-level partitioning (A100/H100), genuine isolation, fixed profile layout
Matching mechanism to requirement: isolation requirement -> MIG; low-stakes small workloads -> time-slicing
Device plugin ConfigMap for time-slicing vs nvidia-smi/MIG profile + GPU Operator for MIG
Training workloads still want a whole GPU regardless; sharing is an inference/multi-tenant-dev concern

Produces working device-plugin ConfigMap + deployment manifests for time-slicing
Produces working MIG enablement + deployment manifest requesting a specific MIG profile
Notes training workloads are out of scope for sharing mechanisms

questions.title: Autoscaling a GPU Inference Endpoint Without Paging On-Call at 3am
questions.prompt: A realtime-inference deployment has a plain CPU-based HPA and never scales up during traffic spikes because its GPU saturates while CPU sits at 5%; when it does eventually scale via another trigger, pods sit Pending for minutes waiting on new GPU nodes. Separately, a bursty-inference workload runs for a few minutes an hour but keeps 3 replicas warm 24/7, burning GPU spend. Fix both: write the correct HPA for the first (scaling on real GPU utilization with pre-warming) and the correct KEDA ScaledObject for the second (scale-to-zero on queue depth), and explain the node-level piece that has to be tuned alongside both or pods keep sitting Pending.
questions.code:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: inference-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: realtime-inference
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Pods
      pods:
        metric:
          name: DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL
        target:
          type: AverageValue
          averageValue: "70"
---
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: bursty-inference-scaler
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    name: bursty-inference
  minReplicaCount: 0
  maxReplicaCount: 5
  triggers:
    - type: prometheus
      metadata:
        serverAddress: http://prometheus.monitoring.svc:9090
        metricName: inference_queue_depth
        query: sum(inference_pending_requests)
        threshold: "5"
questions.example:
# Pod-level scaling is useless if node-level autoscaling can't keep up:
# tune Cluster Autoscaler / Karpenter provisioning speed for the GPU node
# pool alongside both of the above, and use time-slicing/MIG so small
# inference pods don't each demand an entirely new node just to schedule.
questions.modelAnswer: There are two separate mistakes here, one per workload, and they need opposite fixes. The realtime-inference service is scaling on CPU, which is the wrong signal for a GPU-bound model server — it can sit at 5% CPU while its GPU is fully saturated, so the HPA never fires when it actually matters. I'd replace it with an autoscaling/v2 HPA targeting a custom metric sourced from the DCGM exporter through the Prometheus Adapter: DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL as a Pods metric with an averageValue target around 70, and minReplicas: 2 rather than 0 or 1 — that floor is deliberate pre-warming, since this service has a latency SLO and can't absorb a multi-minute cold start while a new GPU node provisions. For the second workload — bursty, a few minutes of real traffic an hour, 3 replicas kept warm the rest of the time — I'd do the opposite: a KEDA ScaledObject with minReplicaCount: 0, maxReplicaCount set appropriately, and a Prometheus trigger on inference_queue_depth with a threshold, so it scales to zero during the idle hours and accepts the cold-start cost on the first request after idle, which is the right trade for genuinely infrequent traffic. Neither fix is complete without touching node-level autoscaling, though — HPA or KEDA deciding to add pods doesn't help if the Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter can't provision a GPU node fast enough, and pods sit Pending for minutes. I'd also apply GPU time-slicing or MIG from the provisioning chapter so small inference pods don't each demand an entirely new node just to get scheduled.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd treat these as two different conversations because the fixes actually point in opposite directions. For the realtime service, the root problem is that CPU utilization just isn't the right signal — I've seen this exact pattern before, GPU pegged at 100%, CPU barely registering, and the HPA sitting there doing nothing because it's watching the wrong number. So I'd wire it to the GPU utilization metric coming out of DCGM through the Prometheus Adapter instead, and I'd keep a minReplicas floor of at least 2 rather than letting it scale to zero, because this one has an SLO and a multi-minute cold start to provision a fresh GPU node is simply not acceptable here. The bursty workload is the opposite case — a few real minutes of traffic an hour, three replicas sitting warm the other fifty-five doing nothing but costing money. That's exactly what KEDA's scale-to-zero is for: a ScaledObject with minReplicaCount: 0 triggered off queue depth, so it only spins up when there's actually something to do. But I'd flag one thing both fixes depend on equally — none of this matters if the cluster autoscaler can't provision a GPU node fast enough, so pod-level and node-level scaling have to be tuned together, and I'd lean on time-slicing or MIG so a small pod doesn't trigger an entire new node just to get scheduled.
commonMistakes: Scales the realtime-inference HPA on CPU utilization, missing that the pod can sit at 5% CPU while its GPU is fully saturated
Sets minReplicas: 0 on the realtime, latency-sensitive workload, introducing unacceptable cold-start latency for an SLO-bound service
Swaps the two patterns — scale-to-zero for the latency-sensitive workload and pre-warming for the truly bursty one
Tunes pod-level autoscaling without touching node-level autoscaling, so pods still sit Pending for minutes waiting for a new GPU node
Forgets GPU utilization must come from the DCGM exporter via Prometheus Adapter to be usable as an HPA custom metric
keyPoints: GPU inference should scale on GPU utilization (DCGM exporter via Prometheus Adapter), not CPU
minReplicas as the simplest form of pre-warming for predictable/latency-sensitive traffic
KEDA enables event/queue-driven scale-to-zero for genuinely bursty, infrequent traffic
Pod-level (HPA/KEDA) and node-level (Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter) autoscaling must be tuned together or pods sit Pending
Matching scale-to-zero vs pre-warming to the right workload's actual traffic shape and SLO tolerance

Correct KEDA ScaledObject with minReplicaCount 0 and a queue-depth trigger for the bursty workload
Explains why CPU-based scaling fails for GPU inference
Identifies and explains the node-level autoscaler tuning needed to avoid Pending pods

questions.title: Designing a Chaos Experiment That Won't Become the Incident It's Testing For
questions.prompt: An SRE wants to validate that payment-service survives a pod failure, but the last attempt — run unannounced at 2am by one engineer — caused a real incident because it killed every pod in the deployment at once with no predefined stop condition. Redesign it correctly: write the Chaos Mesh PodChaos experiment definition with the correct blast radius, and write out the abort criterion and kill-switch procedure that must exist before this runs, plus the scheduling/communication rule that applies.
questions.code:
apiVersion: chaos-mesh.org/v1alpha1
kind: PodChaos
metadata:
  name: pod-kill-payment-service
  namespace: chaos-testing
spec:
  action: pod-kill
  mode: one
  selector:
    namespaces:
      - production
    labelSelectors:
      app: payment-service
  duration: "30s"
questions.example:
#!/bin/bash
# run-chaos-experiment.sh — the gate that must pass before PodChaos is ever applied
set -euo pipefail

# Abort criterion, defined and agreed before the run, not improvised mid-experiment:
#   "if checkout success rate drops below 97% for more than 60 seconds, abort immediately"

echo "Posting experiment announcement to #payments-oncall..."
curl -s -X POST "$SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL" -d '{"text":"Chaos experiment starting: killing ONE payment-service pod in production. Abort if checkout success < 97% for 60s. Kill switch: kubectl delete podchaos pod-kill-payment-service -n chaos-testing"}'

read -p "On-call engineer watching dashboards and confirms ready? (yes/no): " CONFIRM
if [ "$CONFIRM" != "yes" ]; then
  echo "Aborting: no confirmed human watching. Experiment NOT started."
  exit 1
fi

kubectl apply -f pod-kill-payment-service.yaml
echo "Experiment running. Kill switch: kubectl delete podchaos pod-kill-payment-service -n chaos-testing"
questions.modelAnswer: The 2am incident wasn't caused by Chaos Mesh being unsafe — it's caused by skipping every piece of discipline that makes chaos engineering safe in the first place, and the tool just executed exactly what it was told to. I'd fix the blast radius first: the PodChaos resource should use action: pod-kill with mode: one and a tight selector scoped to the production namespace and the payment-service label, so exactly one matching pod dies, not the whole deployment. That's the smallest scope that still answers the real question — does payment-service survive losing a pod — and it's where every first attempt should start, widening only after this smaller version goes well. Before that manifest is ever applied, I'd require two things to exist in writing, not in someone's head: a specific abort criterion — 'if checkout success rate drops below 97% for more than 60 seconds, abort immediately' — and a kill switch, a concrete command like kubectl delete podchaos pod-kill-payment-service -n chaos-testing that anyone running the experiment can execute instantly without a debate about whether things are 'bad enough.' Finally, this runs during business hours, announced in advance to the owning team and anyone else who might get paged, with someone actively watching dashboards in real time, ready to pull that kill switch. An unannounced 2am run with no one watching isn't a rigorous test — it's an unplanned outage someone scheduled on purpose, and that's precisely what happened last time.
questions.professionalAnswer: What actually went wrong last time wasn't the concept — testing if payment-service survives a pod failure is exactly the right thing to want to know. It's that every safety habit around it was missing. So I'd redo this properly: the PodChaos spec itself needs mode: one with a selector scoped tightly to payment-service in production, because the whole point of a first run is the smallest blast radius that still tells you something real — not killing every pod at once. Before I'd let anyone apply that manifest, I'd want two things written down and agreed on beforehand, not decided in the moment: a real abort criterion, something like checkout success dropping below 97% for a full minute, and an actual kill switch — a specific command to delete the chaos resource immediately, not 'we'll keep an eye on it.' And I'd insist this happens during business hours, announced ahead of time so other teams don't mistake it for a real incident, with the owning team actually watching dashboards the whole time. An unannounced run at 2am with nobody watching isn't more rigorous, it's just an outage you caused yourself without any of the safety net that makes the practice worth doing at all.
commonMistakes: Sets mode to kill all matching pods (or omits mode: one) instead of the smallest blast radius that still produces a useful answer
Treats 'we'll watch the dashboards and use judgment' as the abort criterion instead of a specific, measurable, pre-agreed threshold
Runs the experiment unannounced or outside business hours, mistaking surprise for rigor
Has no actual kill-switch mechanism beyond hoping the experiment naturally resolves
Widens blast radius on the very first run instead of starting at mode: one and only expanding after that smaller experiment succeeds
keyPoints: Blast radius: start with the smallest scope that still teaches you something (mode: one)
Abort criterion must be specific, measurable, and defined before the experiment starts
Kill switch is an actual mechanism, not 'judgment'
Run during business hours with the owning team watching, with other teams informed
Chaos Mesh/Gremlin execute the failure precisely; they don't replace the safety discipline around it

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct PodChaos manifest with mode: one and a scoped selector
Defines a specific, measurable abort criterion
Defines an actual kill-switch mechanism/command
Addresses scheduling/communication (business hours, announced, team watching)

questions.title: Computing the Real Blast Radius Instead of Guessing
questions.prompt: Before approving an automated failover for the checkout database, you need the actual blast radius — not what the documented architecture diagram shows, which only lists order-history and pricing-service as downstream of checkout. Write a Python script that computes the full transitive closure of a failure starting at the checkout database, given edge lists from both a documented service-catalog export and discovered dependencies from distributed tracing, and explain why the discovered-edges input matters as much as the documented one.
questions.modelAnswer: The documented diagram showing only order-history and pricing-service downstream of checkout is exactly the trap this exercise is meant to expose — it's what someone intended to build, not necessarily what's actually running. I'd compute blast radius as a real graph traversal, not read it off a diagram. The script loads two edge lists — one from the service catalog export (documented), one from distributed tracing (discovered) — merges them into a single adjacency structure, and then does a breadth-first traversal starting at checkout-db, following edges outward and tracking a visited set so a cycle in the real dependency graph doesn't loop forever. The result is the full transitive closure: everything that calls checkout directly, everything that calls those callers, and so on, not just the first hop. The discovered-edges input matters just as much as the documented one because real dependencies and documented dependencies genuinely diverge — someone adds a 'temporary' synchronous call under deadline pressure, the diagram never gets updated, and six months later that call is permanent and completely invisible to anyone reading the catalog. A trace-derived edge like inventory-service's undocumented call into a legacy warehouse database is exactly the kind of coupling that only shows up by observing real traffic, and skipping it is how a failover decision ships without accounting for a real downstream impact.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the team straight up: the documented diagram answering 'what's downstream of checkout' is the wrong source to trust for a failover decision, because it reflects what someone intended to build, not what's actually running today. So instead of reading it off a picture, I'd compute it — pull the service catalog's documented edges and the distributed-tracing-derived discovered edges into one graph, and run a breadth-first search from checkout-db outward, keeping a visited set so a cycle in the real graph doesn't send the script into a loop. What comes out is the actual transitive closure — everyone affected, not just the services the diagram happens to mention. The reason I'd insist on merging in the discovered edges specifically is that they catch exactly the kind of coupling documentation always misses: a developer wires in a 'temporary' synchronous call that never gets removed, and nobody updates the diagram because nothing broke. Tracing sees that call happen in real traffic whether or not anyone wrote it down. If I'd approved this failover off the documented diagram alone, I'd have missed the legacy warehouse database sitting two hops downstream through inventory-service, and that's exactly the kind of gap that turns a clean failover on paper into a real outage in production.
commonMistakes: Computes only the first-hop neighbors of checkout-db instead of the full transitive closure outward
Builds the graph from the documented service catalog only, missing discovered/undocumented dependencies found via tracing
Doesn't handle cycles in the dependency graph, causing infinite loops instead of using a visited set
Treats the service catalog as a one-time export instead of something refreshed from live trace data regularly
Confuses 'what calls checkout-db' with 'what checkout-db calls,' reversing the direction needed to compute downstream impact
keyPoints: Blast radius = transitive closure of the dependency graph from the failing node outward, not just direct callers
Combine documented (service catalog) and discovered (distributed tracing) dependency sources
BFS/DFS with a visited set to handle cycles and avoid infinite loops
A service catalog accurate at launch degrades over time without being fed live trace data
This computation has to happen before a failover decision ships, automated or human-approved

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct transitive-closure/BFS implementation handling cycles via a visited set
Merges documented and discovered edge sources rather than relying on one
Explains why discovered dependencies catch what documentation misses
Correctly reasons about edge direction for downstream impact

questions.title: Automating Failover Without Recreating the 3am Runbook Problem
questions.prompt: The current DR plan is a wiki runbook a human follows at 3am to fail over the primary region; the last real incident took 40 minutes because the on-call engineer was slow executing steps while fatigued, and one step referenced an endpoint renamed months earlier. Write runbook-as-code that automates failover based on multiple independent health signals (not one flaky check) with a kill switch, and explain which RTO tiers still need a human-approval step versus which require full automation.
questions.example:
# RTO-tier mapping (recommendation, not code):
# 30-min / 5-min RTO  -> automated detection + a human-approval step before promote
# Seconds-level RTO    -> no human step at all; the approval delay IS the SLA breach
questions.modelAnswer: The 40-minute incident has three distinct causes, and automating the runbook only fixes if it fixes all three: slow detection, error-prone execution under fatigue, and a stale runbook referencing a renamed endpoint. I'd write the failover logic as tested, idempotent code rather than a document — a script that polls multiple independent signals, like a synthetic health check and a load-balancer target-health endpoint, and requires every one of them to agree the primary is down for several consecutive intervals before acting, specifically to avoid flapping on one flaky check. It calls out to a separately tested, idempotent promotion script rather than inlining ad hoc commands, so re-running it safely doesn't duplicate work — the same discipline that keeps infrastructure code safe to rerun. I'd build in a kill switch from the start: a simple file or flag the automation checks on every loop, so anyone can disable it instantly without a deploy if it starts misbehaving. On the RTO question, I wouldn't push for full automation everywhere — a human-approval step is still reasonable for most RTO tiers, since a brief pause for a person to confirm doesn't meaningfully hurt a 30-minute or even 5-minute RTO target. Only when the RTO target is genuinely seconds-level does a human-in-the-loop step itself become the bottleneck, which is the one case that strictly requires full automation with no approval gate.
questions.professionalAnswer: When I look at a 40-minute failover that went sideways, I don't see one problem, I see three: it took too long to even notice, the person executing it was tired and under pressure, and one of the steps was just wrong because nobody updated it after an endpoint got renamed. Automating it only helps if it actually addresses all three, not just 'removes the human.' So the script I'd write checks more than one independent signal — a synthetic health check and the load balancer's own view of target health — and only acts once both agree the primary is down for several checks in a row, specifically so one flaky probe doesn't trigger a failover nobody wanted. It calls a separately tested, idempotent promotion step rather than winging commands inline, and it checks a kill-switch file on every loop so I can shut it off in seconds if something looks wrong. The RTO question is the one I'd push back on if someone says 'just automate everything' — for most tiers, a brief human-approval pause costs you almost nothing and buys real judgment before an irreversible regional switch. I'd only drop that approval step entirely if the actual RTO target is seconds, because at that point the human step itself becomes the thing blowing the SLA, not the automation.
commonMistakes: Triggers failover on a single health-check signal, which flaps on a transient blip and causes an unnecessary failover
Builds the failover logic as an ad hoc script that isn't idempotent or tested, recreating the stale-runbook problem in code form
Omits a kill switch entirely, making it impossible to disable the automation quickly if it misbehaves
Assumes every RTO tier needs full automation, when a human-approval step is still appropriate unless RTO is genuinely seconds-level
Hardcodes the automation's own inputs without a process to keep them current, the same staleness problem as the renamed-endpoint wiki runbook
keyPoints: Multiple independent health signals required to avoid flapping/false-positive failover
Runbook-as-code = tested, idempotent code, not a wiki page that goes stale
A kill switch must exist to disable automation quickly
Lower RTO tiers can keep a human-approval step; only seconds-level RTO strictly requires full automation
Three reasons a human 3am runbook is unreliable: slow detection, error-prone execution under fatigue, a stale runbook

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Script requires multiple independent signals to agree before triggering
Script includes a real kill switch mechanism
Script is idempotent/calls a tested promotion step rather than ad hoc commands
Correctly explains which RTO tiers still need human approval vs full automation

questions.title: Recovering from a Lock-Held Terraform State on the S3 Backend
questions.prompt: A CI job crashed mid-apply and now every terraform plan on the shared S3 backend fails with a lock error referencing a stale DynamoDB entry from the dead job. Fix the backend config going forward (it was missing the DynamoDB table entirely) AND safely resolve the current stuck lock. Write the corrected backend block with locking configured, the commands to inspect and resolve the stuck lock, and the one check that must happen before force-unlocking.
questions.example:
# Inspect the stuck lock before touching anything:
terraform plan
# Error acquiring the state lock
# Lock Info:
#   ID:        a1b2c3d4-...
#   Who:       ci-runner-07@github-actions
#   Created:   2026-10-29 03:14:02 UTC

# BEFORE force-unlocking: confirm the job named in "Who" is actually dead, not just slow
gh run list --workflow=terraform-apply.yml --status=in_progress

# Only once confirmed dead:
terraform force-unlock a1b2c3d4-...
questions.modelAnswer: Two separate problems are tangled together here: the backend config was wrong before this incident, and there's a stuck lock right now that needs careful handling, not just a flag flip. The root cause of why a crashed job left a permanently stuck lock is that the s3 backend block never had dynamodb_table set. Unlike azurerm, which gets locking for free from Azure Blob Storage's native lease mechanism, S3 has no equivalent — Terraform's S3 backend only locks at all if you give it a DynamoDB table with a hash key literally named LockID, type String. I'd fix the backend block to include dynamodb_table = "acme-tfstate-locks" going forward, provisioned via its own aws_dynamodb_table resource with PAY_PER_REQUEST billing. For the stuck lock itself, the next terraform plan will print the lock info — Who, Operation, and Created — and that Who field is exactly what has to be checked before anyone force-unlocks anything: confirm, through the CI system directly, that the job named there is actually dead and not just slow. Force-unlocking while that job is still alive risks two concurrent applies writing to the same state simultaneously, which is a real corruption risk, not a theoretical one. Only after confirming the holder is gone would I run terraform force-unlock <lock-id> — and I'd still plan again afterward to check the state itself looks sane, since force-unlock clears the lock record, not the state's correctness.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd point out in the retro is that this was basically inevitable given how the backend was configured — somebody set up backend "s3" without ever adding the DynamoDB table, which means it was never actually locking anything properly on the AWS side the way it would have on Azure, where Blob Storage gives you a lease for free. S3 doesn't have that, so you have to hand it one yourself, and the LockID hash key name isn't optional, Terraform expects it exactly. So that's the config fix. For the lock sitting there right now, I wouldn't touch force-unlock until I'd actually gone and checked whether ci-runner-07, the job named in the lock info, was really dead — I'd pull that up in the CI system directly rather than assume. Running force-unlock while that job might still be alive is how you get two applies hitting the same state at once, and that's a much worse day than a stuck lock. Once I've confirmed it's gone, then force-unlock, and I'd still run a plan right after just to sanity-check the state wasn't left half-written by the crash — clearing the lock doesn't tell you anything about whether the state file itself is still trustworthy.
commonMistakes: Omits dynamodb_table from the s3 backend block, not realizing S3 has no native lease mechanism the way azurerm's Blob Storage does
Runs terraform force-unlock immediately without checking whether the job named in Who is actually still running
Assumes force-unlock itself resolves any partial/corrupted state left by the crashed apply, when it only clears the lock record
Creates the DynamoDB table with an arbitrary hash key name instead of LockID, which Terraform's S3 backend requires exactly
Confuses terraform force-unlock with terraform state rm/import, applying the wrong recovery command for a lock problem versus a state-drift problem
keyPoints: S3 backend needs a separate DynamoDB table (dynamodb_table arg, hash key LockID type String) because S3 has no native lease
azurerm backend locks automatically via Azure Blob Storage's native lease — the asymmetry worth knowing
Lock error output shows Who/Operation/Created, which is what you check before force-unlocking
force-unlock only safe after confirming the lock holder isn't still running
force-unlock clears the lock record; it doesn't validate or fix the underlying state file

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct S3 backend block with dynamodb_table and correct DynamoDB table schema (LockID)
Correct force-unlock command used appropriately
Explains the required check (confirm holder is dead) before force-unlocking
Notes the azurerm-vs-s3 locking asymmetry as the root cause of the missing config
